paper_metadata.title: Unsupervised quantum machine learning for fraud detection

summary: The paper studies fraud detection on a 500-sample credit-card dataset with 25 fraud cases, comparing classical logistic regression, RBF SVC, and RBF OC-SVM against IQP quantum-kernel methods with up to 20 qubits/features. In simulation, the quantum kernels reach about 0.9 average precision for supervised classification and about 0.7 for unsupervised anomaly detection at 20 qubits, corresponding to roughly a 15% improvement over the classical OC-SVM benchmark.

experiments.description: Supervised fraud detection using quantum kernels (IQP feature map with data re-uploading) on a credit card fraud dataset, compared against classical logistic regression and RBF SVC baselines.

algorithm.variant: quantum kernel classification with IQP feature map and data re-uploading

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Each feature is scaled and embedded into one qubit; number of qubits equals number of features (principal components).
problem_formulation.objective_function: Binary classification of fraud vs genuine transactions using kernel-based support vector classification in feature Hilbert space.

problem_instance.description: Credit card fraud detection on a public Kaggle dataset, using PCA-reduced features and varying feature count from small sizes up to 20.

dataset_specification.description: 28 anonymized features; time and amount ignored; subsampled to 500 total samples including 25 fraud examples; PCA applied after standard scaling; features varied to match qubit count.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Feature-wise standard scaling, PCA dimensionality reduction, keep first N principal components, scale features by eta=0.1 for quantum embedding.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average precision (AP) evaluated as a function of number of features/qubits; compared against classical benchmarks.

implementation_details.classical_solver: scikit-learn SVC with RBF kernel; logistic regression baseline

speedup_claims.factor: greater than 10% average precision improvement at >10 qubits; about 15% at 20 qubits
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical logistic regression and RBF SVC
speedup_claims.conditions: supervised fraud classification on the subsampled Kaggle credit card dataset with PCA features up to 20 qubits and IQP re-uploading quantum kernels
speedup_claims.caveats: This is an empirical performance separation, not a proven computational speedup; results are from statevector simulation.
No asymptotic quantum speedup is proven.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Kernel evaluation scales as O(N_s^2) for full Gram matrix; inference for Nd new samples scales as O(N_d N_s).
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical kernel methods also require O(N_s^2) Gram matrix evaluation.
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Not specified; paper discusses stronger separation at larger feature counts, reaching 20 qubits.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Around 20 qubits/features in simulation; authors suggest stronger separation may appear at 50-100 qubits.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Statevector simulation on NVIDIA A100 GPU; no real quantum hardware used.
limiting_factors: No QPU experiment; only noiseless simulation
Empirical separation is modest and problem-specific
Classical baselines are strong and sometimes comparable at smaller feature counts
Kernel evaluation and data loading scale poorly for large datasets

notes: hardware.type inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states state vector simulation and uses PennyLane/JAX on GPU, with no real QPU device named.
circuit depth not explicitly quantified; only the feature-map structure and re-uploading count d=3 are reported.
speedup_order marked none_proven because the paper reports empirical separation but no asymptotic quantum speedup proof.
The paper reports better average precision for quantum kernels at larger feature counts, but this is only in simulation and not a demonstrated practical advantage.

experiments.description: Unsupervised fraud detection using quantum kernels with one-class SVM (OC-SVM) and IQP feature map with data re-uploading, compared against classical RBF OC-SVM baseline.

algorithm.variant: unsupervised quantum kernel anomaly detection with OC-SVM and IQP feature map

hyperparameters.ocsvm_gamma: 1/(NVar[X]) for classical baseline; quantum kernel bandwidth tuned implicitly by eta=0.1

problem_formulation.objective_function: Novelty detection / anomaly detection: separate nominal transactions from anomalous fraud samples using one-class SVM in quantum feature space.

problem_instance.description: Credit card fraud detection on a public Kaggle dataset, using only nominal data for OC-SVM training and evaluating anomaly detection on fraud-labeled test data.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average precision (AP) versus number of features/qubits; labels used only for evaluation/plotting, not training.

implementation_details.classical_solver: scikit-learn one-class SVM with RBF kernel

speedup_claims.conditions: unsupervised anomaly detection on the subsampled Kaggle credit card dataset with IQP re-uploading quantum kernels and OC-SVM
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a performance advantage in average precision, not a runtime or asymptotic complexity speedup; results are from statevector simulation.
